summary: Describes version 0 of the Ogg bitstream format, a freely available container that can hold any number of audio, video, and other data streams in one stream. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Ogg packages encoded media into pages, so several streams can share one bitstream and later be separated again. Its page markers and checksums help a reader find boundaries and detect damaged data.

what is an ogg page header
subtitle: How Ogg packages media packets into pages that can be checked, interleaved, and recovered.

tldr.problem: Media encoders produce packet streams that need boundaries, error detection, and a way to combine several streams. Ogg provides this framing without depending on a particular codec.
tldr.mechanism: Ogg divides packets into segments, groups them into pages, and interleaves pages from logical streams in one physical bitstream. Page headers carry stream identifiers, position information, sequence numbers, and a checksum.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3533 describes Ogg bitstream format version 0 as an Informational document. Codec-specific media mappings define how encoded media uses the container.

today: RFC 3533 is an Informational RFC describing Ogg bitstream format version 0. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Purpose of Ogg Encapsulation
sections.content:
Ogg is a general encapsulation format for media streams. It supplies framing, error protection, seeking landmarks, and a way to recover synchronization after a parsing error, while remaining independent of the codec that created the media packets.

The format can combine packets from one or more encoders in a single physical bitstream. The RFC's design aims include streaming without seeking, simple parsing and concatenation, and overhead of approximately 1-2 percent. Ogg packets are encoder-defined units, not network packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Ogg adds boundaries and checks around media data without interpreting the codec itself. A reader can use those boundaries to separate the original packets and find its place after an error.

sections.title: Logical Streams, Pages, and Multiplexing
sections.content:
A logical bitstream is the ordered packet stream produced by one encoder. A physical bitstream contains pages from one or more logical bitstreams. Each page identifies its logical stream with a serial number, and each logical stream begins with a beginning-of-stream page and ends with an end-of-stream page.

Ogg supports grouping, which interleaves pages of multiple logical streams, and chaining, which places complete physical bitstreams one after another. In a grouped stream, all beginning pages appear before data pages. Ogg position values are codec-dependent landmarks, not a general measure of time; a media mapping defines their meaning and any audio/video synchronization.
sections.plainLanguage: Each encoded stream keeps its own order, while Ogg can mix its pages with pages from other streams. The format can also place complete streams one after another.

sections.title: Turning Packets into Segments and Pages
sections.content:
Ogg splits a packet into segments of up to 255 bytes, with a shorter final segment when needed. A page contains a group of contiguous segments and a header with a segment table. A lacing value of 255 means the packet continues; a value below 255 ends the packet after that many bytes.

A packet whose size is an exact multiple of 255 bytes uses a final lacing value of zero to mark its end. A zero-length packet is valid and has a zero lacing value. The segmentation scheme avoids imposing a maximum packet size, while keeping small-packet overhead low.
sections.plainLanguage: Ogg cuts each packet into segments no larger than 255 bytes, then records segment lengths in the page header. A special zero value can mark the end of a packet that fills an exact number of segments.

sections.title: The Ogg Page Header
sections.content:
Each page starts with the four-byte capture pattern OggS. The fixed header also contains a version, page flags, an eight-byte granule position, a logical-stream serial number, a page sequence number, a CRC checksum, and the number of segment-table entries. The header length is the segment count plus 27 bytes.

The continuation flag shows whether the page begins with a packet continued from the previous page. Other flags identify the first and last pages of a logical stream. The sequence number helps detect lost pages, while the CRC checks the page header and content. Multi-byte fields are encoded least-significant byte first.
sections.plainLanguage: The page header starts with OggS and identifies the stream and page. Its sequence number and checksum help a reader notice missing or damaged pages.

sections.title: Security and Content Handling
sections.content:
Ogg is a container and does not provide general encryption or signing for itself or its contents. An Ogg bitstream can carry encrypted or signed data, and an external security mechanism can protect a complete physical bitstream.

Because Ogg carries binary data, a stream can contain executable content. The RFC says the container itself does not create that threat, but applications that decode Ogg must handle manipulated streams and buffer overflows correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Ogg does not encrypt or authenticate its contents. Software that reads an Ogg stream still needs to handle malformed data safely.

viz.caption: FIXED FIELDS IN AN OGG PAGE HEADER

fields.name: Capture pattern
fields.desc: Marks the beginning of a page.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Ogg file-format version; this RFC describes version 0.

fields.name: Header flags
fields.desc: Marks continuation, beginning of stream, or end of stream.

fields.name: Page segments
fields.desc: Number of entries in the segment table.
